title: Package tracking
brief: You run the tracking page for a parcel company. People refresh it again and again while they wait for a delivery, and depots send a scan every time a parcel moves. Keep the page fast, lose at most the last minute of scans in a failure (scanners keep a copy and can resend), and make sure a broken text-message service cannot slow anything down.

clarify.q: Do tracking answers have to be up to the second?
clarify.a: No. A status that is up to a minute old is fine. People care that the page opens fast and the next step is right.

clarify.q: Can a depot scan be lost or counted twice?
clarify.a: At most the last minute of scans, and only in a failure: scanners keep a copy and resend when the network drops, so the same scan can arrive twice. Counting it twice would show the wrong history.

clarify.q: What happens when the text-message service is down?
clarify.a: Alerts can arrive later. The tracking page must keep working and no alert may be dropped.

notes: About 15 million parcels a day, 8 scans each, about 0.5 KB per scan: roughly 60 GB a day, 90 days kept hot (approx.).
Reads are tracking-page lookups, writes are depot scans, notifications are text and push alerts.
The peak is a holiday-season evening. All numbers are rough approximations.

numbers.label: Reads that reach the database with an 85% cache hit rate
Scan history kept for 90 days
numbers.how: 15M parcels x 8 scans x 0.5 KB = 60 GB a day, x 90 days

hints: Most of the load is people checking the same parcel again and again. What could remember an answer for a minute?
A cache between your servers and the database turns most lookups into memory reads. Send alerts through a queue so a failing alert service cannot slow the page.
Cache with a 60 second keep time and collapse misses. Four servers over two zones, a queue with two workers into the push service, and an idempotency store so a repeated scan counts once.

editorial.summary: This is a read-heavy problem with a small, careful write path. Nine in ten requests are lookups of data that changes a few times a day, so a cache answers most of them. Scans are the data you cannot lose, and alerts are work that can wait, so they go through a queue.

designs.name: Cached lookups, queued alerts
designs.why: A short-lived cache takes about 85 percent of lookups off the database. The network balancer costs almost nothing per request. Alerts wait in a queue, so when the push service fails for twenty minutes they are sent afterwards and the tracking page never notices.

designs.name: Fully managed, pay for every call
designs.why: Serverless functions and a key-value table need almost no operations work and scale on their own. At this steady, high volume you pay for every single call, so the bill is far above the budget. It is a good choice for a small parcel company and a poor one for a large one.

tradeoffs: A 60 second cache means a status can be a minute old. For parcels that is fine; for a stock price it would not be.
Collapsing misses protects the database when the cache is cold, at the price of a few people waiting for one shared refill.
A queue adds a small delay to alerts and in return makes a failing push service harmless.
The idempotency store costs a little per scan and prevents a duplicate scan from rewriting history.
Fully managed services trade your time for their per-call price. Check the bill at peak, not just at launch.
editorial.realWorld: Large parcel companies track on the order of tens of millions of parcels a day and answer many more lookups than scans. Most of those lookups are served from caches (approx.).
